meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I have never understood why it is greed to want to keep the money you have earned but not greed to want to take somebody else's money'?
meta.ogDescription: Thomas Sowell really wrote it: a May 1994 syndicated column, reprinted in Barbarians inside the Gates (1999). Here is the source trail.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: born 1930 · American economist and social theorist
answer.sourceLine: Sowell wrote it in a syndicated newspaper column in May 1994. Barry Popik cites the Tuscaloosa News of 13 May 1994, where it ends “someone else’s money.” He reprinted it word for word, ending “somebody else’s money,” in Barbarians inside the Gates and Other Controversial Essays (Hoover Institution Press, 1999). A full-text search of that book confirms the wording.

source.excerpt: I have never understood why it is “greed” to want to keep the money you have earned but not greed to want to take somebody else’s money.
trail: Barry Popik traces the line to a syndicated column Sowell wrote in May 1994. He cites the Tuscaloosa (AL) News, 13 May 1994, p. 6A, col. 4, where it ends “someone else’s money” (Barry Popik ↗).

A full-text search of the 1999 Hoover Institution Press edition of Barbarians inside the Gates and Other Controversial Essays finds the sentence word for word, ending “somebody else’s money” (Internet Archive ↗).
Wikiquote lists the line under Barbarians inside the Gates and Other Controversial Essays (1999) on its Thomas Sowell page (Wikiquote ↗).
A different line that circulates beside it, about “need,” “greed” and “compassion,” is Joe Sobran’s. Popik cites it from The Economics of Liberty (1990) (Barry Popik ↗).
source.excerptNote: This is the wording in the 1999 book, the version that circulates today. The 1994 newspaper printing, as Barry Popik transcribes it, ends “someone else’s money.” In the book, the next item begins “What an irony that Richard Nixon was dying…”

author.name: Thomas Sowell
author.heading: About Thomas Sowell
author.metaLine: Born 1930 · American economist, social theorist & Hoover Institution senior fellow
author.bio: Thomas Sowell was born in Gastonia, North Carolina, and grew up in Harlem. He served in the Marine Corps during the Korean War. He then graduated from Harvard, earned a master’s at Columbia and a PhD in economics at the University of Chicago. He is a senior fellow at the Hoover Institution and received the National Humanities Medal in 2002. Readers know him best for his books and his syndicated newspaper columns, many of which were later collected in essay volumes such as Barbarians inside the Gates.

misattribution.heading: What gets mixed up
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Sowell holds. Two things do get mixed up: a small change in the wording between printings, and an older line by a different columnist that people often quote alongside it.

items.why: Popik’s transcription of the 13 May 1994 Tuscaloosa News column ends “someone else’s money.” The 1999 book reads “somebody else’s money,” the form most sites quote today. Popik reproduces both (Barry Popik ↗).

“‘Need’ now means wanting someone else’s money. ‘Greed’ means wanting to keep your own. ‘Compassion’ is when a politician arranges the transfer” is a shortened form of a passage by Joe Sobran. Popik cites it from The Economics of Liberty (Mises Institute, 1990), p. 169. Popik calls Sowell’s line “a similar quote,” but the wording is Sobran’s, not Sowell’s (Barry Popik ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Thomas Sowell wrote it in a May 1994 syndicated column and reprinted it in Barbarians inside the Gates and Other Controversial Essays (1999) (Barry Popik ↗).

context.heading: Why it travels
lead: This is one of Sowell’s most-shared lines in arguments about taxes and redistribution. Barry Popik notes that it “has been frequently cited by conservative authors.” One example he records is a post by U.S. Representative John Fleming on 8 August 2012 that credits it to Barbarians inside the Gates (Barry Popik ↗).

Unlike many lines credited to Sowell online, this one is accurate. The wording that circulates today matches his 1999 book exactly. The Foundation for Economic Education uses the same wording in its list of Sowell quotations (FEE ↗).

sourcesVerified.claim: Popik cites a Sowell syndicated column of May 1994, Tuscaloosa (AL) News, 13 May 1994, pg. 6A, col. 4, ending "someone else's money". He also says the line appeared in Barbarians inside the Gates (1999), notes it is frequently cited by conservative authors, and records Rep. John Fleming's Facebook post of 8 Aug 2012.

Barbarians inside the Gates--and Other Controversial Essays, Thomas Sowell, Hoover Institution Press, 1999. Internet Archive full-text search of this item returns the sentence ending "not greed to want to take somebody else's money", followed by "What an irony that Richard Nixon was dying".
Wikiquote's Thomas Sowell page lists the line under Barbarians inside the Gates and Other Controversial Essays (1999).
Popik traces the need/greed/compassion line to Joe Sobran, The Economics of Liberty (Mises Institute, 1990), p. 169, and calls Sowell's line "a similar quote".
FEE's list of Sowell quotes includes the line with the book wording ("somebody else's money").

Thomas Sowell was born June 30, 1930, is a Hoover Institution senior fellow and received the National Humanities Medal in 2002. He grew up in Harlem, served in the Marines during the Korean War, and studied at Harvard, Columbia and the University of Chicago.
